summary: Suggests a pair of TCP options for using alternate data checksum algorithms in the TCP header. The use is experimental and not recommended in production. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1146 and RFC 6247.

eli5.summary: Packets have a check number to catch mistakes. This lets two computers agree to use a different way of computing that check number.

subtitle: Letting TCP connections negotiate different data checksum algorithms.

tldr.problem: TCP's standard checksum uses a simple 16-bit algorithm that has limited error detection properties. Some applications want stronger checksums or checksums that detect different types of errors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1145 defines two TCP options: one to negotiate an alternate checksum algorithm during connection setup, and another to carry checksums larger than 16 bits if needed.
tldr.outcome: The option remains experimental and not recommended for production use, as the underlying problem has not been widely adopted.

today: RFC 1145 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1146 and RFC 6247.

sections.title: Why Alternate Checksums
sections.content:
TCP's checksum is a 16-bit one's complement sum. This catches many errors, but some applications need better error detection, or checksums that detect particular types of corruption, such as transposition of bytes. RFC 1145 provides a mechanism for two TCP implementations to agree to use a different checksum algorithm instead of the standard one.

The protocol is experimental. Alternate checksums remain negotiable only during connection setup (the SYN and SYN-ACK segments always use the standard TCP checksum for compatibility). If the two sides cannot agree on the same algorithm, they fall back to the standard checksum.
sections.eli5: The standard check number works for most cases, but some programs want a better one. This lets them pick a different kind as long as both sides agree.

sections.title: The TCP Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines two TCP options. The TCP Alternate Checksum Request Option (kind 14, length 3) carries a one-byte identifier specifying which algorithm to use. The currently defined algorithms are type 0 (standard TCP checksum), type 1 (8-bit Fletcher algorithm, producing a 16-bit checksum), and type 2 (16-bit Fletcher algorithm, producing a 32-bit checksum).

The TCP Alternate Checksum Data Option (kind 15) holds the checksum when it is longer than 16 bits. It appears only in the first fragment. For checksums longer than 16 bits, the implementer can choose to split the checksum between the TCP header field and the option, or put it entirely in the option with the header field set to zero.
sections.eli5: The first option says which kind of check to use. The second option holds the check number if it is too long for the header.

sections.title: Negotiation and Operation
sections.content:
Negotiation happens during the SYN exchange. If both the SYN and the responding SYN-ACK carry the Alternate Checksum Request option and both specify the same algorithm, that algorithm is used for the entire connection. Otherwise, the standard checksum is used. This ensures backward compatibility: an implementation that does not support the option will ignore it and both sides will use the standard checksum.

Any segment with the SYN or RST bit set must always use the standard checksum. The alternate checksum begins only with the first non-SYN segment. An error in the checksum format (wrong data length for the algorithm) causes a reset and connection abort.
sections.eli5: The two computers agree on which check type at the start. If they agree, they use it. If not, they use the standard one. SYN messages always use the standard to make sure both sides understand.
